title: 60 Senators Killed the Most Powerful Man in Rome
titles: 60 Senators Killed the Most Powerful Man in Rome
Caesar Was Warned. He Went Anyway.
The Murder That Destroyed the Roman Republic
description: On the Ides of March, 44 BC, more than sixty Roman senators stabbed Julius Caesar 23 times, men he had pardoned and promoted. This is the true story of Caesar's rise from a kidnapped young noble to dictator for life, the warnings he ignored, the murder under Pompey's statue, and how killing him to save the Republic created Rome's first emperor.
sources: Suetonius, The Life of Julius Caesar
Plutarch, Life of Caesar and Life of Brutus
pinned_comment: Were the senators heroes or traitors? Pick a side.

scenes.say: On the morning of the fifteenth of March, 44 BC, the most powerful man in the world walked into a meeting of the Roman Senate. He had conquered Gaul, won a civil war, and been named dictator for life. Within minutes, he was lying dead on the floor.

search: Jean-Léon Gérôme The Death of Caesar
visuals.ai: Caesar lying dead in an empty Roman hall, painting
an ancient marble bust of Julius Caesar
a marble Roman meeting hall

scenes.say: He wasn't killed by an enemy army. He was killed by more than sixty senators. Men he had pardoned. Men he had promoted. One of them, a man he treated almost like a son.

visuals.ai: senators surrounding Caesar with daggers, painting

scenes.say: This is the true story of how Julius Caesar rose higher than any Roman before him, why the men around him decided he had to die, and how the murder that was meant to save the Roman Republic ended up destroying it.

visuals.ai: the ruins of the Roman Forum

scenes.say: To understand why they killed him, we have to start with the man himself. And with one story that tells you everything about him.

visuals.ai: a marble bust of Caesar in a museum

scenes.say: When Caesar was about twenty five, he was sailing across the Aegean Sea when pirates captured his ship. They told him his ransom was twenty talents of silver. Caesar laughed at them. He said he was worth at least fifty, and told them to ask for more.

visuals.ai: an ancient warship with oars
blue sea between Greek islands

visuals.label: Talents of silver, his own ransom
visuals.note: Plutarch: the pirates asked for 20, Caesar insisted on 50

scenes.say: For more than a month he lived with them as if he were their boss. He read them his poems, told them to be quiet when he wanted to sleep, and joked that one day he would come back and crucify them all. They thought it was funny.

visuals.ai: an ancient scroll
pirates on a rocky island, painting

scenes.say: When the ransom was paid and he was free, Caesar raised a small fleet, hunted the pirates down, took back the money, and did exactly what he had promised. That was Julius Caesar. He always kept his word. Especially his threats.

visuals.ai: a fleet of Roman ships at sea

scenes.say: Back in Rome, Caesar understood something the old families didn't. Power came from the crowds. So he spent money like no one else. He paid for games, gladiators and feasts, and borrowed to do it.

visuals.ai: gladiators in a Roman arena, painting
a Roman banquet, painting

scenes.say: At one point, he owed so much money that his creditors tried to stop him leaving Rome. The richest man in the city, Marcus Crassus, stepped in and guaranteed his debts. Caesar was betting everything on one idea. Once he had power, the money would come back.

visuals.ai: a marble bust of a Roman nobleman
a pile of Roman silver coins

scenes.say: In 60 BC he made a secret deal with the two most powerful men in Rome. Crassus, the richest. And Pompey the Great, the most famous general alive. Together, the three of them ran Rome from behind the scenes. Historians call it the First Triumvirate. To seal it, Caesar gave Pompey his only daughter, Julia, as a wife.

visuals.ai: three Roman leaders, ancient coins

scenes.say: He was right. In 58 BC, he took command in Gaul, modern France. For eight years he fought there. He won battle after battle, and sent home so much treasure and so many slaves that his name was on every Roman's lips.

search: Vercingetorix throws down his arms Lionel Royer
visuals.ai: a Gallic chief surrendering to Caesar, painting
an old map of ancient Gaul

scenes.say: Then the deal began to fall apart. In 54 BC, Julia died in childbirth, and the family tie between Caesar and Pompey was gone. A year later, Crassus marched east to fight the Parthians and was killed at Carrhae. A famous legend says his enemies poured molten gold into his mouth, to mock his greed.

visuals.ai: ancient horse archers in the desert
molten gold being poured

scenes.say: But in Rome, the Senate was getting nervous. A general that rich, that popular, with an army that loyal to him personally, was the most dangerous thing a republic could have.

visuals.ai: a Roman senator speaking in the Senate, painting

scenes.say: In 49 BC the Senate ordered him to give up his army and come home as a private citizen. Caesar knew that if he did, his enemies would put him on trial and finish him.

visuals.ai: Roman soldiers in armour

pops.label: the line no general could cross

scenes.say: There was a small river in northern Italy called the Rubicon. It marked the border. No general was allowed to cross it with his army. To do so meant war against Rome itself.

visuals.ai: a small river in northern Italy

scenes.say: According to the ancient writers, Caesar stood at the river, hesitated, and then said, the die is cast. And he crossed.

visuals.ai: Caesar on horseback crossing a river, painting

visuals.by: Julius Caesar at the Rubicon, 49 BC (Suetonius)

scenes.say: The civil war that followed lasted years. His great rival Pompey, once his friend and even his son in law, fled to Greece, lost the battle of Pharsalus, and escaped to Egypt.

search: Pompey the Great bust Ny Carlsberg
visuals.ai: a marble bust of Pompey the Great

scenes.say: When Caesar arrived in Egypt, the Egyptians handed him a gift. Pompey's head. They thought he'd be pleased. The ancient writers say Caesar turned away and wept.

search: head of Pompey presented to Caesar
visuals.ai: a Roman general looking away from a gift, painting
the ancient harbour of Alexandria

scenes.say: In Egypt, he met the young queen Cleopatra, and they had a son. By 46 BC, Caesar had beaten every enemy in the Roman world. He came home as the master of everything.

visuals.ai: an ancient marble bust of Cleopatra
a Roman victory parade, painting

scenes.say: And he changed Rome in ways we still live with. He fixed the broken Roman calendar and gave it three hundred sixty five days with a leap year every four years. The month of his birth was renamed after him. July.

visuals.ai: an ancient carved Roman calendar

scenes.say: And here's where the trouble really began. Rome hated kings. Almost five hundred years earlier, the Romans had thrown out their last king and sworn never to have another one.

visuals.ai: an ancient bronze head of a stern Roman

scenes.say: In an emergency, the Republic could name a dictator, but only for six months. Caesar was named dictator for ten years. Then, in February 44 BC, dictator for life.

visuals.title: How long a dictator could rule
visuals.note: In 44 BC he became dictator for life

scenes.say: His face appeared on coins while he was still alive, something no living Roman had done before. He sat on a golden chair in the Senate. He filled the Senate with his own supporters, raising it to nine hundred members.

search: Julius Caesar denarius portrait coin 44 BC
visuals.ai: an ancient silver coin with Caesar's face
an ancient Roman official chair

visuals.label: Senators, after Caesar packed the Senate

scenes.say: Then, at a festival in February, his ally Mark Antony tried to place a royal crown on his head in front of the crowd. Caesar pushed it away. Antony offered it again. Again, Caesar refused. The crowd cheered. But many senators wondered. Was it a refusal, or a rehearsal?

visuals.ai: a marble bust of Mark Antony
a Roman festival crowd, painting

scenes.say: Quietly, a group of senators started meeting in secret. They called themselves the Liberators. Their plan was simple. Kill Caesar, and give Rome back its freedom.

visuals.ai: a dark Roman house at night
an ancient clay oil lamp burning

scenes.say: The leader was Gaius Cassius, a sharp, angry soldier who had fought against Caesar in the civil war, and been pardoned by him.

visuals.ai: an ancient coin of a Roman senator

scenes.say: But Cassius needed a name the people would trust. He needed Marcus Brutus. Brutus came from the family of the man who had thrown out Rome's last king. And his mother, Servilia, had been one of Caesar's great loves.

visuals.ai: a marble bust of a serious young Roman
a marble bust of a Roman noblewoman

scenes.say: Caesar had pardoned Brutus after the war, given him top jobs, and protected him. Some people in Rome even whispered that Brutus was Caesar's own son. Historians think that's unlikely, but it shows how close they were.

visuals.ai: a row of Roman marble busts in a museum

scenes.say: The plotters also had a deadline. Caesar was planning a huge war in the east, and he would leave Rome on the eighteenth of March. Once he was with his army, nobody could touch him. It had to be done before he left.

visuals.ai: a Roman army on the march, painting

scenes.say: And there was a third man, the one Caesar trusted most of all. Decimus Brutus, a general who had fought beside him in Gaul. His job in the plot would be the cruelest of all. Making sure Caesar came to the meeting.

visuals.ai: a statue of a Roman general in armour

scenes.say: Caesar had been warned. A soothsayer named Spurinna had told him to beware of danger that would come no later than the Ides of March, the fifteenth day of the month.

visuals.ai: an ancient Roman priest reading signs

scenes.say: On the night before, his wife Calpurnia had a nightmare. She dreamed she was holding his body in her arms. In the morning she begged him not to go. For a while, he agreed to stay home.

visuals.ai: a Roman woman waking from a nightmare, painting
a painted Roman room

scenes.say: Then Decimus Brutus arrived at his house. He told Caesar the senators were waiting, and that it would look weak to send them home because of his wife's dream. Caesar took his hand, and went.

visuals.ai: an ancient Roman street

scenes.say: There was one more thing that made it possible. A few months earlier, Caesar had sent away his personal bodyguard. He said it was better to die once than to live always afraid of dying.

visuals.ai: an ancient carving of Roman guards

scenes.say: On the way, a man pushed a scroll into his hand. It listed the names of the conspirators. Caesar held it, meaning to read it later. He never did.

visuals.ai: an ancient Roman wax writing tablet

scenes.say: As he passed the soothsayer, Caesar joked, the Ides of March have come. The soothsayer answered, yes, they have come. But they have not gone.

visuals.text: The Ides of March have come. ... Yes, they have come, but they have not gone.

scenes.say: The Senate wasn't meeting in its usual building that day. It met in a hall attached to the great theatre built by Pompey, the rival whose head Caesar had wept over. Inside stood a statue of Pompey.

visuals.ai: an ancient Roman theatre complex
a marble statue of Pompey

scenes.say: Outside the door, one of the plotters, Trebonius, stopped Mark Antony and kept him talking. Antony was strong and loyal. They didn't want him inside.

visuals.ai: a Roman colonnade

scenes.say: Caesar sat down. A senator named Tillius Cimber came forward, asking him to pardon his brother. The others crowded around as if they were supporting him. Then Cimber grabbed Caesar's toga and pulled it from his neck. That was the signal.

visuals.ai: a marble statue of a man in a toga

search: Karl von Piloty murder of Caesar
visuals.ai: senators rushing at Caesar, painting

scenes.say: A senator named Casca struck first, and missed, only cutting his neck. Caesar grabbed his arm and shouted at him. Then the others closed in, from every side.

visuals.ai: an ancient Roman dagger

scenes.say: According to Suetonius, Caesar was stabbed twenty three times. A doctor who examined his body later said only one of those wounds, the second, to his chest, was fatal.

visuals.label: Wounds
visuals.note: Suetonius; a doctor said only one was fatal

search: Death of Caesar painting Theodor Mommsen
Death of Julius Caesar 19th century painting
visuals.ai: a dramatic painting of Caesar's murder

scenes.say: When he saw Brutus among them, the ancient writers say he stopped fighting. He pulled his toga over his face and fell at the foot of Pompey's statue. Some said his last words, in Greek, were, you too, child? Shakespeare later made it famous as et tu, Brute. But Suetonius says he may have said nothing at all.

visuals.by: Reported by Suetonius, who doubted it

scenes.say: Julius Caesar was fifty five years old. The most powerful man in the world lay dead at the feet of the rival he had beaten.

The Liberators ran out into the streets, holding up their daggers, shouting that Rome was free. They expected the people to cheer. Instead, the city went silent. People locked their doors. Nobody cheered.

visuals.ai: the Roman Forum, painting

scenes.say: And then the conspirators made their biggest mistake. They let Mark Antony live, and they allowed Caesar a public funeral.

visuals.ai: a statue of Mark Antony

scenes.say: At the funeral, Antony read out Caesar's will. Caesar had left his gardens to the public, and money to every single citizen of Rome. Three hundred sesterces each.

visuals.ai: a crowd listening to a speech over a body, painting

visuals.label: Sesterces left to every citizen
visuals.note: Suetonius; Plutarch gives 75 drachmas, about the same

scenes.say: Then Antony held up Caesar's bloody toga, with every tear from every dagger. The crowd exploded. They built a fire in the middle of the Forum, burned Caesar's body there, and ran through the city with torches, looking for the killers.

search: Roman Forum Temple of Caesar ruins
visuals.ai: ancient ruins in the Roman Forum
burning torches at night

scenes.say: Cleopatra, who was living in Rome with their young son, quietly packed up and sailed home to Egypt. Without Caesar, Rome was no longer safe for her either.

visuals.ai: Cleopatra and Caesar, painting

scenes.say: Brutus and Cassius had to flee Rome. The men who called themselves liberators were now hunted.

visuals.ai: an old Roman road at dusk

scenes.say: In his will, Caesar had named an heir. Not Antony. His eighteen year old great nephew, Octavian. Almost nobody took the sickly young man seriously.

visuals.ai: a marble bust of a young Roman

scenes.say: That summer, during games held in Caesar's honour, a bright comet appeared in the sky for seven days. Octavian told the people it was Caesar's soul rising to join the gods. Rome believed him. Caesar became a god.

visuals.ai: a bright comet in the night sky
an ancient coin with a star

scenes.say: Octavian joined forces with Antony. Together they hunted the conspirators across the Roman world.
In 42 BC, at Philippi in Greece, their armies met the armies of Brutus and Cassius. Cassius, believing the battle was lost, took his own life. Weeks later, after a second defeat, so did Brutus.

visuals.ai: an ancient battlefield in Greece
a defeated Roman general, painting

scenes.say: Suetonius wrote that none of Caesar's killers lived more than three years after his death, and that none of them died a natural death.

visuals.text: Hardly any of his assassins survived him for more than three years, or died a natural death.

scenes.say: And here's the final twist. The senators killed Caesar to stop Rome from having a king. Seventeen years later, Octavian took the name Augustus, and became Rome's first emperor. The Republic they died for never came back.

visuals.ai: a marble statue of the emperor Augustus

scenes.say: Brutus even made coins to celebrate the murder. On one side, two daggers and a cap of freedom. Under them, the words EID MAR. The Ides of March. In 2020, a gold one sold at auction for more than three million pounds.

visuals.ai: an ancient silver coin with two daggers

scenes.say: And the spot where Caesar fell? Today it's a sunken square of ruins in the middle of Rome called Largo di Torre Argentina. It is home to a sanctuary for stray cats. They sleep among the stones where the most famous murder in history happened.

visuals.ai: ancient ruins in a square in Rome
cats sleeping on ancient Roman stones

scenes.say: So what does the death of Caesar teach us about power? First. The most dangerous people are rarely your enemies. Caesar pardoned the men who killed him. He trusted the man who walked him to his death.

visuals.ai: marble hands from an ancient statue

scenes.say: Second. Power without limits always creates enemies. The moment Caesar became dictator for life, every ambitious man in Rome had a reason to want him gone.

visuals.ai: the old Roman Senate house

scenes.say: And third. Killing a leader doesn't kill an idea. The Liberators thought one morning of violence would fix everything. Instead, they made Caesar a god, and handed Rome to an emperor.

visuals.ai: Rome at sunset
